summary: Mobbin studied nearly 3,000 paywalls and hundreds of subscription flows, and interviewed Jonathan Parra, who has designed over 4,700 paywalls, to find what separates high-performing paywalls from average ones. The main lessons are that a paywall is a flow, not a single screen: it should sell the outcome first, appear at the right moment in the customer lifecycle, and reduce the fear of being charged with trial timelines, reassuring subtitles and longer trials. Some findings run against intuition: added friction such as requiring a credit card can raise paid conversion, and an ugly, text-heavy paywall sometimes beats a beautiful one, so there is no universal best paywall, only better experiments. It also covers pricing and packaging (default to yearly, show only two plans), framing techniques (social proof, value framing, price anchoring), formats (multi-page, table, video) and the tactics to be wary of, such as spin-the-wheel offers, fake urgency and free-trial toggles that Apple began rejecting. For a design system this gives concrete patterns, copy and component choices for subscription screens, plus a warning that conversion patterns must be tested and weighed against long-term trust, retention and LTV.
key_ideas: A paywall is a flow, not a screen: the product should sell the outcome before it asks for money, so the paywall feels like the natural next step.
Users sometimes decide to pay before they even see the paywall, so every touchpoint in the lifecycle matters.
Paywalls can appear after onboarding, when unlocking a premium feature, inside settings, or as a win-back offer before the user leaves.
A well-designed paywall shown at the wrong moment is still a bad paywall.
Multi-page paywalls, where information unfolds gradually, almost always beat single-page paywalls in Jonathan's experience.
Some of the best-performing paywalls reduce perceived risk: a step-by-step trial timeline, a 'no commitment, cancel anytime' subtitle, or a longer trial.
Presentation can change results even when the offer does not change.
More friction can raise paid conversion: requiring a credit card for a trial filtered out people who were never serious.
Common framing techniques are social proof, value framing matched to what users care about, and price anchoring.
Default to a yearly plan for the highest LTV, show only two plans, and hide any others behind a 'view all plans' sheet.
Tables show what users miss if they don't subscribe; video can communicate value faster than screenshots or bullet points.
Polish (animation, custom characters, world building) is becoming a differentiator now that anyone can ship an app.
Spin-the-wheel paywalls and fake urgency can maximise short-term revenue but wear down trust; users learn to close paywalls to get an offer.
There is no universal best paywall; radically different design tests move the needle most.
Retention and LTV matter more than getting the first payment.

entities.name: Mobbin
entities.description: Maker of the video; studied the paywalls and subscription flows in its library.

entities.name: Jonathan Parra
entities.description: Guest known as 'The Paywall Guy', who has designed over 4,700 paywalls for consumer apps.

entities.name: Superwall
entities.description: Paywall tool; Jonathan learned from Jake and Nick there that design tests move the needle most, and says tables are hard to build in it.

entities.name: RevenueCat
entities.description: Named alongside Superwall as a place where Jonathan is not seeing many table paywalls.

entities.name: Opal
entities.description: Sells the outcome (getting 8 years of your life back) before its paywall; trial sign-ups rose from 7% to 17%.

entities.name: Ahead
entities.description: Unfolds paywall information gradually and compares its price to coffee or therapy.

entities.name: Blinkist
entities.description: Added a step-by-step trial timeline after users felt tricked into being charged.

entities.name: Tipstop
entities.description: Emphasised the free trial and added a discount badge; direct conversions almost tripled (name as heard in the captions).

entities.name: Slopes
entities.description: Replaced the paywall with a 'pay ramp' single action, raising trial starts by 25%.

entities.name: Apple
entities.description: Its redeem-free-trial approach inspired Slopes; in early 2026 it began rejecting paywalls that relied on free-trial toggles.

entities.name: Outsider
entities.description: Required credit card details to start a trial: fewer sign-ups, far higher conversion.

entities.name: Moonly
entities.description: Offered a free trial only on the annual plan.

entities.name: Tide
entities.description: Anchors price by breaking it into smaller weekly amounts.

entities.name: Headspace
entities.description: Tested 7-, 14- and 30-day trials; a 14-day trial on the annual plan won.

entities.name: Focus Town
entities.description: App Jonathan cites for polish: branding and an Animal Crossing-esque experience.

entities.name: ClassPass
entities.description: Takes fewer than five screens to subscribe but 17 to cancel.

entities.name: Lottie
entities.description: Animation file format used for the predetermined spin-the-wheel paywall.

entities.name: Pay ramp
entities.description: Slopes' replacement for a paywall: one action, 'redeem your free week'.

entities.name: Exit intent sheet
entities.description: A sheet shown when the user tries to cancel, offering a smaller commitment such as the monthly plan.

entities.name: Price anchoring
entities.description: Framing price as small weekly amounts or against familiar spending.

entities.name: LTV
entities.description: Lifetime value [inferred: the source never expands the acronym]; with retention, the metric Jonathan wishes founders cared about most.

topics.name: A/B testing and conversion
topics.summary: Case results (Opal 7% to 17%, Slopes +25%, Outsider five times conversion, Headspace 14-day winner) and the conclusion that radically different design tests move the needle most; there is no universal best paywall.

topics.name: Onboarding
topics.summary: The paywall at the end of onboarding should feel like a natural segue: 'your plan is ready', framed around the user's ideal outcome.

topics.name: Dark patterns and user-hostile design
topics.summary: Spin-the-wheel offers, fake urgency and aggressive last-minute discounts can work short term but erode trust; Apple began rejecting confusing free-trial toggles.

topics.name: Content and microcopy
topics.summary: A 'no commitment, cancel anytime' subtitle helps; a CTA naming what the user is doing instead of 'Continue' is hit or miss; value framing and price anchoring are copy choices.

topics.name: Drawers and sheets
topics.summary: Extra pricing plans go behind a 'view all plans' button that opens a sheet; an exit intent sheet offers the monthly plan when the user tries to cancel.

topics.name: Retention and gamification
topics.summary: Retention and LTV are the metrics that matter most; the goal is building something worth paying for, not only getting the first payment.

topics.name: Mobile app patterns
topics.summary: Consumer-app subscription patterns: trial timelines, one-time offers with animation and haptic feedback, video paywalls and Apple's review stance on trial toggles.

quotes: A paywall isn't just a screen. It's a flow.
there is literally no universal best paywall, only better experiments.
When every app uses fake urgency tactics, users eventually stop believing it.

rules.rule: Sell the outcome before the paywall (for example, how much time or life the user gets back), so the paywall reads as the natural next step of the flow rather than an interruption.
rules.why: Opal's trial sign-ups rose from 7% to 17% after showing users how many years of their life they could save; a working paywall feels like the product asking for the next step.
rules.evidence: [1:25] Before asking for money, Opal spends time selling the outcome

rules.rule: Prefer a multi-page paywall that unfolds information gradually over a single-page paywall that shows everything at once.
rules.why: Multi-page paywalls almost always do better in Jonathan's experience, and gradual information gives users time to process the decision.
rules.evidence: [1:46] Multi-page paywalls almost always do better than single-page paywalls

rules.rule: At the end of onboarding, make the paywall a natural segue that finishes onboarding: tell the user their plan is ready and speak to their ideal outcome in emotional terms (for example, feeling like themselves in 4 weeks).
rules.why: The paywall should already feel part of the experience.
rules.evidence: [2:10] Does the paywall already feel part of the experience?

rules.rule: Show a step-by-step timeline of the free trial on the paywall screen.
rules.why: Blinkist users felt tricked into being charged; the timeline brought more trial sign-ups, fewer complaints, and more push notification opt-ins.
rules.evidence: [3:14] redesigned the paywall screen to show a step-by-step timeline

rules.rule: Add a 'no commitment, cancel anytime' subtitle to the paywall's call to action.
rules.why: It always seems to do well and bumps conversion up incrementally.
rules.evidence: [4:12] This no commitment cancel anytime subtitle always seems to do well

rules.rule: Experiment with a call-to-action label that names what the user is doing instead of a plain 'Continue'.
rules.why: Jonathan finds it hit or miss, so he tests it.
rules.evidence: [4:22] kind of call to action for what the user is doing instead of just continue

rules.rule: Consider putting a right chevron on the paywall's main button.
rules.why: Most winning paywalls in Jonathan's experience have one, though he has not tested it in isolation.
rules.evidence: [4:33] having this right chevron here on the button

rules.rule: When a user tries to cancel or close a yearly offer, show an exit intent sheet that offers the monthly plan instead.
rules.why: Users not ready to commit for a year can still subscribe monthly.
rules.evidence: [5:01] I like to show the users an exit intent sheet

rules.rule: Don't use aggressive last-minute discounts (except perhaps for Cyber Monday or Black Friday); offer a longer free trial instead.
rules.why: A larger trial keeps you compliant and safe and can achieve the same goal while preserving trust.
rules.evidence: [5:13] I wouldn't really do this unless it's maybe Cyber Monday Black Friday

rules.rule: Default the paywall to the yearly plan unless a yearly product doesn't suit your business.
rules.why: Yearly products have the highest LTV.
rules.evidence: [7:17] you want to default to a yearly product

rules.rule: Show only two plans on the base paywall (the yearly plan plus a weekly or monthly one) and put any other plans behind a 'view all plans' button that opens a sheet.
rules.why: Showing two decreases cognitive load on the user.
rules.evidence: [7:30] You only want to show two to decrease cognitive load

rules.rule: Launch a simple base paywall and measure its base stats before optimising different placements.
rules.why: You need baseline performance before going further with optimisation.
rules.evidence: [7:42] You want to keep the base paywall simple

rules.rule: Consider a table-based paywall that shows users what they miss out on if they don't subscribe.
rules.why: Tables do a good job of showcasing what you miss by not subscribing; Jonathan is a huge fan of them.
rules.evidence: [7:58] I am a huge fan of tables

rules.rule: Consider a video paywall that shows the app in action, with a simple bullet list and simple social proof.
rules.why: Video can communicate value faster than static screenshots or bullet points.
rules.evidence: [8:10] A video paywall showing you the app in action

rules.rule: Make the free trial prominent, add a discount badge, and make the offer easier to understand.
rules.why: Tipstop's direct conversions almost tripled with the same offer presented this way.
rules.evidence: [3:32] emphasized the free trial, added a discount badge

rules.rule: Use price anchoring: break the price into smaller weekly amounts or compare it with things people already spend money on, such as coffee or therapy.
rules.why: It is one of the framing techniques the studied paywalls use (Tide, Ahead).
rules.evidence: [6:40] And then there's price anchoring

rules.rule: Show social proof on the paywall with real user reviews and a five-star rating.
rules.why: Social accolades show credibility and authority.
rules.evidence: [6:14] most common techniques is social proof

rules.rule: Time a one-time offer (gone once closed) to the moment the user is considering an upgrade, and pair it with animation and haptic feedback.
rules.why: A well-designed paywall at the wrong moment is still a bad paywall; animation and haptics help pull the user's attention at the moment they are considering an upgrade.
rules.evidence: [2:45] One example is the one-time offer

rules.rule: If you're building for the long term, avoid spin-the-wheel paywalls and fake urgency.
rules.why: They can maximise weekly-price revenue, but when every app uses fake urgency users stop believing it, and users learn to close paywalls expecting an offer.
rules.evidence: [10:06] If you're optimizing for a longer-term business, that may not be a good paywall for you

rules.rule: Don't build paywalls around free-trial toggles.
rules.why: In early 2026 Apple started rejecting paywall patterns that relied on them because some were considered confusing or misleading.
rules.evidence: [10:37] Apple also started rejecting paywall patterns that relied on free trial toggles

rules.rule: Test radically different paywall designs (video, bullet list, trial timeline, long-form) against each other, then test copy, pricing and flow until one clearly wins.
rules.why: Design tests move the needle the most, and an ugly paywall can beat a beautiful one; there is no universal best paywall.
rules.evidence: [11:16] design tests move the needle the most

rules.rule: Plan paywalls across the whole customer lifecycle (after onboarding, when a premium feature is unlocked, inside settings, and as a win-back offer before the user leaves), and show each one at the right moment.
rules.why: All the touchpoints are extremely important, contextual paywalls speak more to the user because they're more personalized, and a well-designed paywall at the wrong moment is still a bad paywall.
rules.evidence: [0:59] Those paywalls speak more to the user because they're more personalized.

rules.rule: Consider offering a longer free trial on the annual plan; Headspace's 14-day trial for the annual plan beat 7-day and 30-day trials.
rules.why: Even though the annual plan costs more, the longer trial made the whole decision feel less risky.
rules.evidence: [7:00] The winning variant was this, 14-day trial for the annual plan

rules.rule: Don't assume removing friction raises paid conversion: consider requiring payment details to start a free trial, to filter out people who are not serious.
rules.why: When Outsider required credit card details, sign-ups dropped by more than half but conversion rates rose five times and paying customers more than doubled; the extra friction filtered out people who were never serious.
rules.evidence: [5:56] The extra friction filtered out people who were never serious

rules.rule: Frame the paywall's value around what the user cares about, so it sells the future that user wants.
rules.why: Value framing is one of the common framing techniques; the studied screens are all selling different futures.
rules.evidence: [6:31] You're framing the value in such a way that it matches what the users care about

rules.rule: Consider replacing the traditional paywall with a pay ramp: one action, such as 'redeem your free week'.
rules.why: Slopes built this, inspired by Apple's redeem-free-trial approach, and it alone increased trial starts by 25%.
rules.evidence: [3:57] a pay ramp. Users see a single action, redeem your free week.

rules.rule: Put time into polish: animations, custom character designs and world building.
rules.why: Now that anyone can ship an app the bar has been raised; Jonathan expects the most polished apps to be the most successful, and polish could be why someone chooses your product over others.
rules.evidence: [8:50] put in the time to polish it with animations, with custom character designs

rules.rule: Judge subscription work by retention and LTV, not only by how many people subscribe.
rules.why: Jonathan wishes founders cared most about retention and LTV: if they are good you are building a good product, and building something people keep paying for is much harder than getting them to subscribe.
rules.evidence: [11:45] The metrics that I wish more founders really care the most about is retention and LTV

caveats: Self-promotion: Mobbin plugs its own Mobbin MCP at [9:05], and the description links to the guest's X account and tapasgrowth.com.
Case results (Opal, Blinkist, Tipstop, Slopes, Outsider, Headspace) are single-company outcomes quoted without test details, sample sizes or dates; they are not general benchmarks.
Many recommendations are one practitioner's experience ('I like to', 'almost always'); the right chevron is explicitly untested in isolation, and the CTA wording is 'hit or miss'.
Dated information: published 2026-07-09; Apple's early-2026 rejection of free-trial toggles and its handling of Black Friday sales may change.
Auto-caption spellings: 'Moby' at [0:03] is Mobbin and 'A Head' at [2:19] is Ahead (spelled 'Ahead' at [6:45]); the names Tipstop, Moonly, Tide and Outsider are as heard and not verified.
The description is cut off ('Previously, he worked at Superwa'); the transcript only confirms he learned from Jake and Nick at Superwall.
Moonly's result is not stated; the video only says it 'discovered something similar'.
The video is highly visual; the on-screen paywall examples are only partly described in the transcript and no media list was available.
Spin-the-wheel, fake urgency and aggressive discounts are described as working short term; the source presents them as patterns not worth copying, not as recommendations.
